evidence_pointers.quote: deterministic apply/merge ordering rules independent of wall-clock completion timing

decision_log.question: How should integration conflicts beyond deterministic resolution thresholds be handled?
decision_log.choice: Conflicts below a configurable threshold are auto-resolved by the Integration Patcher (C21) within bounded op caps. Conflicts above the threshold trigger HITL escalation with a structured conflict_report.
decision_log.rationale: This balances speed (auto-resolve simple conflicts) with safety (escalate complex conflicts). The threshold and op caps are orchestrator-owned policy, ensuring deterministic behavior. This directly implements the K12 mitigation and the branch's risk posture of accepting integration complexity with focused HITL at the integration level.
alternatives_considered: Always escalate all conflicts to HITL: rejected as too slow for the speed-oriented branch posture.
Never escalate (fully automated resolution): rejected as too risky for complex merge scenarios.
Reroute to Planning Council for re-partitioning: considered as a secondary escalation path if HITL cannot resolve.
what_would_change_this_decision: If automated conflict resolution proves unreliable, requiring all conflicts to go to HITL.
If conflict rates are so low that the threshold mechanism adds unnecessary complexity.

evidence_pointers.quote: strict limits for automated conflict resolution; if limits exceeded, block and trigger reroute to integration stage or HITL

decision_log.question: Should partial freeze be supported in this candidate?
decision_log.choice: No. If budgets are exhausted before integration completes, the orchestrator checkpoints with a stage_handoff for deterministic resume rather than producing an incomplete freeze bundle.
decision_log.rationale: The branch's acceptance strategy requires two levels of validation (lane-level and integration-level) before freeze. A partial freeze would bypass integration validation, undermining the governance model. Checkpoint-and-resume preserves all completed work without compromising freeze integrity. O3 is the architecture designed for partial freeze; O2's strength is parallel speed to full completion.
alternatives_considered: Support partial freeze with completion_status metadata (O3-style): rejected because it conflicts with the branch's integration-focused acceptance strategy.
Allow freeze of completed lanes only: rejected because it would produce an incomplete, non-integrated bundle.
what_would_change_this_decision: If long-horizon execution becomes a primary concern and full completion within budget is frequently infeasible.
If downstream consumers can meaningfully consume partially-integrated bundles.

evidence_pointers.quote: the final integrated state must pass a full suite of system-level validators and an integration review before the freeze is accepted

decision_log.question: What governance posture should be applied to tooling and HITL?
decision_log.choice: Sandboxed tooling with medium HITL strictness, focused on integration-level findings and critical security/compliance events.
decision_log.rationale: Per branch B02 specification: sandboxed tooling level and medium HITL strictness. This means lane-level execution relies more on automated validation with HITL reserved for integration conflicts, security critical findings, ChangeRequests, and gate waivers. This balances speed (fewer HITL interruptions during parallel lanes) with safety (human oversight at the critical integration fan-in point).
alternatives_considered: High HITL strictness at every stage: rejected as incompatible with parallel speed goals.
Low HITL strictness: rejected as insufficient for integration risk management.
what_would_change_this_decision: If security/compliance requirements mandate HITL at every lane-level review.
If integration conflict rates are very low, allowing further HITL reduction.

decision_log.question: How should context packs be scoped for parallel lanes vs integration?
decision_log.choice: Lane context packs are compiled from lane-scoped workspace partitions only. Integration context packs include cross-lane artifacts selected by deterministic priority rules with configured token/byte bounds.
decision_log.rationale: Lane-scoped context packs keep per-lane context small and focused (an O2 advantage). Integration context packs must span lanes but are bounded by explicit selection rules to prevent context overflow (K9 mitigation). The orchestrator (C11) owns compilation rules for both.
alternatives_considered: Global context packs for all stages: rejected due to context window pressure.
Unbounded integration context packs: rejected due to K9 risk.
what_would_change_this_decision: If cross-lane dependencies are frequent, requiring broader context in lane stages.
If model context windows grow large enough to make bounding unnecessary.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Integration Risk Assessment for O2
supplemental_evaluations.notes: The primary risk of O2 is at the integration fan-in (K12). The branch explicitly accepts this trade-off. Mitigations include: (1) deterministic merge ordering by task ID, (2) conflict thresholds with HITL escalation, (3) full-repo revalidation at integration, (4) dedicated integration reviewer and patcher roles. The risk is further reduced by the work plan compiler (C12) which partitions tasks to minimize file-set overlap. Residual risk: tightly-coupled repos with high file overlap will experience frequent conflicts, potentially negating parallel speed gains. Monitoring metric: conflict rate per integration cycle.

glossary.definition: A CouncilOS subsystem that consumes a frozen planning output (plan_package_final.json) and produces audited, reproducible repository changes and release artifacts under orchestrator-controlled policies and validators.

The canonical, typed/versioned set of JSON artifacts emitted at freeze, including run manifest, event log, work plan, patchsets, repo snapshot, test/quality/trace/review/release artifacts, decision record, and required workspace artifacts (workspace_index, context_packs, stage_handoffs).

A tool-accessible, versioned and auditable storage area treated as an extension of the artifact system, containing canonical JSON artifacts and explicitly non-canonical notes/summaries, governed by permissions, retention, and checkpoint/resume handoffs.

An RFC 6901 JSON Pointer object {artifact_ref, entity_id|null, json_pointer, note} referencing a versioned JSON artifact location; used as the sole standard for traceability across decisions, findings, and state representations.

A required JSON artifact emitted at each checkpoint boundary capturing resumable state: objectives, completed work, pending blockers, next actions, and pointers into canonical artifacts (work plan, patchsets, validation outputs).

A canonical artifact proposed when plan semantics would need to change; requires explicit decisioning and policy-triggered escalation (HITL and/or reroute upstream) before any semantic deviation is allowed.
Deterministic code component with sole authority over routing, budgets, iteration limits, termination, checkpoint/resume, tool permissions, selection logic, and validator enforcement.
A bounded, deterministically-compiled set of workspace artifacts provided to a role at a stage, selected by explicit rules and cited via evidence pointers.
A JSON artifact embedding code diffs with deterministic apply order for repo modifications; used as the sole mechanism for code repair/changes in the workflow.
A code-owned deterministic gate that checks artifact integrity/completeness and quality criteria to allow stage transitions or freeze.
